verses.text: I tell the truth in Christ—I'm not lying. My conscience confirms it through the Holy Spirit:
I carry deep sorrow and unending pain in my heart.
I could wish that I myself were cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers and sisters, my own people by human descent.
They are Israelites. Theirs are adoption, glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, worship, and the promises.
The patriarchs belong to them, and from them, in his human ancestry, came the Messiah, who is God over all, praised forever. Amen.
But God's word hasn't failed. Not everyone descended from Israel truly belongs to Israel.
And not all of Abraham's descendants are his children. Rather, Scripture says, ‘Your descendants will be traced through Isaac.’
That means physical descendants aren't automatically God's children. The children of the promise are counted as Abraham's offspring.
For this is the promise: ‘At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.’
And that's not all. Rebekah also became pregnant by one man, our father Isaac.
Before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, God's purpose in choosing could stand—not because of works, but because of the one who calls.
Rebekah was told, ‘The older will serve the younger.’
As Scripture also says, ‘I loved Jacob, but I rejected Esau.’
So what should we say? Is God unjust? Absolutely not!
God told Moses, ‘I will show mercy to whomever I choose to show mercy, and compassion to whomever I choose to show compassion.’
So it doesn't depend on what someone wants or tries to do, but on God, who shows mercy.
Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘I raised you up for this very purpose: to show my power through you and make my name known throughout the earth.’
So God shows mercy to whom he chooses, and he hardens whom he chooses.
You might ask me, ‘Then why does God still blame people? Who can resist what he wants?’
But who are you, a human being, to argue back to God? Can what was made say to its maker, ‘Why did you make me like this?’
Doesn't a potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one pot for honored use and another for ordinary use?
What if God, wanting to show his anger and make his power known, patiently endured objects of anger prepared for destruction?
And what if he did this to make the riches of his glory known to objects of mercy, which he prepared in advance for glory—
including us, whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles?
As God says in Hosea: ‘I will call those who were not my people my people, and the one who was not loved my beloved.’
‘And where they were told, You are not my people, they will be called children of the living God.’
Isaiah cries out about Israel: ‘Even if the number of Israel's children is like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved.
For the Lord will carry out his word on earth, completely and without delay.’
And as Isaiah said earlier, ‘If the Lord of Armies hadn't left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.’
So what should we say? Gentiles who weren't pursuing righteousness received it—the righteousness that comes through faith.
But Israel, pursuing a law meant to bring righteousness, didn't reach that goal.
Why? Because they pursued it as if it came from works instead of faith. They stumbled over the stumbling stone,
just as Scripture says: ‘Look, I am placing in Zion a stone that makes people stumble, a rock that trips them up; but whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.’
